items.q: Design a feature-flag and A/B experimentation system on the client
items.prompt:
Design the client-side of a feature-flag system: remote flags that can turn features on/off and serve A/B variants to cohorts, with kill switches and exposure logging.

Assume ~10M DAU, an Android client, flags change multiple times a day, and some flags gate critical paths (payments, login). **Set a 45-minute timer and talk out loud.** Tick the requirements as you genuinely cover them.
items.framework: This scenario is lighter than most — it's the client half of an infrastructure product. Run the standard framework but expect the interviewer to push hardest on **staleness vs availability** (what the app does when the flag payload is missing) and **evaluation consistency**.
requirements: Clarify who reads flags and how often
Define the flag evaluation API surface
Design the config payload and its versioning
Choose sync: fetch on start, poll, or push; and failure behaviour
Cache flags locally and survive cold start
Handle the first-run and logged-out case
Define how cohorts/rollouts map to a user
Design the kill switch path for a critical flag
Cover exposure logging and bucketing consistency
Talk about consistency across devices for the same user
Specify what happens when a flag is removed
Cover observability and the flag-serving dashboard
Mention experimentation hygiene: assignment must not correlate with the metric
Close with explicit trade-offs
items.referenceAnswer:
#### Architecture

Three parts: a small client SDK embedded in the app, a config service that returns flag payloads, and the experiment/assignment layer that decides which variant a user gets. `App code → FlagClient.eval("pay_v2") → cached payload + resolver`, fed by a `config fetch (work manager) ← config service` on the side.

#### The payload
Each flag is `{ key, type, value, targeting }`. Targeting encodes the experiment assignment: `{ experiment, variant, rule }`. A rule is evaluated against user attributes (`user_id`, `country`, `app_version`, `install_date`). A sticky bucketing rule: `hash(user_id + experiment_id) % 100` lands the user in a bucket, and buckets map to variants. **Stickiness is the hard requirement** — the same user must stay in the same variant across sessions or the experiment is noise. Payload shape: `{ "flags": [ { "key": "checkout_v2", "type": "boolean", "value": true, "targeting": { "experiment": "co_ab", "rule": "hash(id)%100 < 40" } } ], "version": 42, "ttl": 600 }`.

#### Sync strategy
- **Cold start**: a bundled default payload must exist so the app renders without the network. Startup never blocks on config.
- **Refresh**: WorkManager with a network constraint, respecting an incremental sync (config only fetches changed keys via version).
- **Push**: a quiet FCM topic per app version for urgent kill switches, so critical flags flip in seconds.
- **Missing payload**: `eval` falls back to the bundled default and logs a miss; a critical flag that is missing should **fail closed** (safe default) by configuration.

#### Kill switch
A critical flag (e.g. "payments_paused") must be evaluable even if the main config fetch is broken, so it rides the push channel. The dashboard allows one-tap global override that takes effect on the next eval — for truly urgent cases a push forces the client to re-eval immediately.

#### Exposure logging
When `eval` runs and the flag gates something meaningful, the client logs `{user, experiment, variant, timestamp}` through the analytics SDK (see sd-0004). The logging itself must be sampled and batched or it becomes a second product. Log-before-eval consistency matters: log what you actually *served*, using the same bucketing inputs, or the analyst gets garbage.

#### Experimentation hygiene
- Assignment must be **exogenous**: the bucketing hash inputs must not be influenced by the treatment.
- Guardrails: a dashboard with 'did the flag actually ship to the intended %', 'did the variant corrupt a core metric', and automatic rollback thresholds.
- Version pinning: cohorts are defined at assignment time; upgrading the app mid-experiment must not reassign a user.

#### Failure modes
- Config service down → serve cached + bundled defaults, log misses, keep the last-known-good.
- Corrupt payload → schema-validate and refuse to apply.
- Clock skew → use server-issued timestamps for TTL.
- Flag removed → clients self-heal on next fetch, but a transition window must let the code path drain.

#### Trade-offs to close with
Local cache adds staleness risk but buys offline and cold-start. Push gives speed but adds a channel. Sticky bucketing buys statistical validity at the cost of slow variant ramp. You'd also mention: staged rollout of the SDK itself behind a flag, and treating flags as code with PR review.
rubric: Defined a clean eval API and payload schema
Designed sync with bundled defaults and offline fallback
Made bucketing sticky and explained why
staffAdds: Quantifies: 'a flag evaluated on every frame would cost 10k evals/s on-device — so hot flags are cached in memory and cold flags are read from disk'
Plans the migration: how an existing if/else tree is replaced flag-by-flag
Considers the analytics pipeline end-to-end and the lag before an experiment is readable
Proposes automatic rollback thresholds tied to crash-free sessions and core metrics
Designs the SDK interface so flags can be owned by different product teams with separate review

items.q: Design a crash-reporting and observability SDK
items.prompt:
Design a mobile crash-reporting and observability SDK (think a Firebase Crashlytics / Sentry class product): capture crashes and ANRs, attach context, and upload without hurting the app.

Assume tens of millions of devices, mixed Android versions, and privacy constraints (GDPR/CCPA). **Set a 45-minute timer and talk out loud.** Tick the requirements as you genuinely cover them.
items.framework: This is a client-infrastructure scenario. Expect the interviewer to probe **what to capture** (breadcrumbs, threads, memory) and **upload policy** (network, quota, retry) harder than the backend pipeline.
requirements: Clarify what events to capture: crash, ANR, native, custom
Design the capture hooks (Thread.UncaughtExceptionHandler, ANR detection)
Decide how much context to attach: threads, memory, breadcrumbs, logs
Design on-device buffering and the upload policy
Handle the app restart flow and the 'crash on startup' case
Discuss sampling and rate limiting
Cover privacy: PII stripping, consent, data minimization
Design the upload retry with backoff and jitter
Talk about symbolication for native and release builds
Design the backend pipeline briefly (ingest, store, dashboard)
Address performance cost of the SDK on the main thread
Cover ANR detection specifics (input dispatch, broadcast, service)
Name observability metrics: crash-free sessions, severity
Close with explicit trade-offs
items.referenceAnswer:
#### Architecture

The SDK has three planes: capture, buffer, upload. Capture must never block the app's main thread; buffer must survive process death; upload must be bandwidth-aware and never interfere with the user. Flow: `App crash → UncaughtExceptionHandler → session serializer → file buffer`, then on next launch `Uploader (WorkManager) → ingest API`.

#### Capture
- **Java/Kotlin crash**: install a `Thread.UncaughtExceptionHandler` that logs the report to a file *synchronously enough to survive the process dying*, then calls the previous handler. This is the famous 'file must hit disk before the process dies' problem — the handler has milliseconds.
- **Native crash**: register the `debuggerd` callback or use the platform crash handler; native frames need symbolication from uploaded `.so` symbols.
- **ANR**: no exception fires. Options: `ApplicationExitInfo` (API 30+, reason == `REASON_ANR`), or a watchdog thread on `InputDispatcher`. `ApplicationExitInfo` is the modern answer and is cheap.
- **Custom**: breadcrumbs — ring buffer of last ~100 app events with timestamps, attached to the report.

#### What to attach
Thread dump (with stack traces and thread states), memory class + heap headroom, app version, OS, device model, the breadcrumbs, and a session id. Strip anything identifying: redact URLs, truncate exception messages at a size budget, and never send raw files by default.

#### Buffering and upload
Reports are serialized to a directory and indexed in memory; on process death the directory is the only truth. Upload via WorkManager with a `NetworkType.CONNECTED` constraint, **not metered if possible**, with exponential backoff + jitter (ds-0059) capped at a day. A per-day quota (e.g. 200 reports) and sampling (1-in-k of non-critical events) bound cost.

#### Crash-on-startup loop
If the app keeps crashing at startup, uploading fails too. Mitigation: a 'crash loop' detector that, after N same-signature crashes at startup, sends a minimal report with a flag and stops trying.

#### Privacy
PII stripping by default, a consent gate that can disable collection, local data minimization, and a documented retention policy. The SDK must be usable in a privacy-first mode where only anonymized aggregate counts leave the device.

#### Backend sketch
Ingest API (validate + schema-check) → raw store → symbolication pipeline → normalized events in a queryable store → dashboard + alerting. Alerts keyed on crash-free sessions per version, not raw crash counts, which punish installs.

#### The performance contract
No work on the main thread. Capture is a few microseconds; serialization is off-thread; the buffer is append-only so it's cheap. Measure SDK overhead as a first-class metric — a crash SDK that adds jank is itself a bug.
rubric: Chose the right capture hooks and explained the process-death window
Handled ANR without a watchdog if possible (ApplicationExitInfo)
Designed disk-backed buffering surviving process death
Gave a bandwidth-aware upload policy with backoff
staffAdds: Quantifies the crash-on-startup window: 'the handler has ~1 s before the kernel reclaims us; a malloc in the handler can fail, so the buffer is pre-allocated'
Designs the ingest pipeline capacity around a spike: 'an outage spikes crash rate 50x — the ingest must shed load without dropping critical reports'
Considers multi-team ownership: how feature teams add their own breadcrumbs without forking the SDK
Plans a schema versioning story for the report format
Defines rollback via the kill-switch channel (sd-0005)

items.prompt:
Design an image-loading library like Coil or Glide: given a URL and a target size, load a bitmap from memory cache, disk cache, or network, then decode, transform, and display it — all without janking the UI.

Assume Android + Compose (but discuss Views interop), mid-range devices, and mixed networks. **Set a 45-minute timer and talk out loud.** Tick the requirements as you genuinely cover them.
items.framework: A contained, high-signal scenario. The interviewer will push on the **request lifecycle** (cancellation, reuse, keying) and the **memory cache** — that's where Coil/Glide earn their keep.
requirements: Clarify the API surface you'd expose
Design the request pipeline (load → decode → transform → display)
Explain how a request is keyed for caching
Design the memory cache and its size policy
Design the disk cache and eviction
Handle multiple sizes of the same image
Handle cancellation and request reuse (LazyColumn fling)
Design the background executor / dispatchers
Cover the placeholder / error / success states
Decode at the right sample size to avoid OOM
Cover prefetching
Handle animation / transitions
Mention what happens on activity recreation
Close with explicit trade-offs
items.referenceAnswer:
#### API surface
Keep it small and declarative: `Image(url, size, placeholder, error)`. The library reads a request: `{ url, targetSize, scale, transformations }`. In Compose, `remember` + the state holder do the lifecycle; in Views, the loader attaches to the view's lifecycle.

#### Pipeline stages
1. **Key**: `url + targetWidth + targetHeight + scaleType + transformations` hashed to a single cache key. The *size* must be in the key — two screens showing the same URL at different densities need different bitmaps.
2. **Memory cache lookup** — the hot path, sub-millisecond.
3. **Disk cache lookup** — decoded bytes, re-decode off the main thread.
4. **Network fetch** with an HTTP client (Coil uses OkHttp), streaming into the disk cache first.
5. **Decode** with `BitmapFactory.Options.inSampleSize` computed from target size and image dimensions, so a 4K image is never fully decoded for a 100 px target. Actually downsample to nearest power of two and let the display tier do the final scale.
6. **Transform** (crop, round corners, blur) via `Bitmap` or, on newer APIs, `ImageDecoder`.
7. **Display** with a crossfade handled at the Composable level.

#### Memory cache
Sized off `ActivityManager.memoryClass` (e.g. 1/8), using an `LruCache` keyed on the request key, counting `byteCount`. Hold strong references to in-use bitmaps and weak references otherwise — never recycle aggressively, because the same bitmap may be on screen in multiple places. On `onTrimMemory`, evict the LRU first.

#### Disk cache
A directory with an LRU eviction policy and a size budget (say 200 MB), keyed by the request hash, storing the *encoded* bytes so different target sizes of the same source don't duplicate storage. Disk reads go to a dedicated dispatcher, never the main thread.

#### Concurrency and cancellation
The load runs on `Dispatchers.IO` (or a bounded pool); the result is delivered on the main thread. **Cancellation is the hard part.** In a flinging `LazyColumn`, requests are made and cancelled at ~50 Hz; each request carries a token, and when a new request for the same key supersedes an in-flight one, the old one is cancelled and its coroutine's job is cancelled so stale results never land on the UI. Reuse: two composables showing the same key share one in-flight request (single-flight, ds-0018).

#### Placeholder/error/success
A state machine per request: `Loading → Success | Error`. Placeholder and error drawables are cached; a failed request can be retried with backoff, and the error state remembers so it doesn't hot-loop.

#### Prefetch
`Image.prefetch(url, size)` warms memory+disk without a target view — used for the next scroll page or a detail screen.

#### Failure modes
Disk cache corruption (treat as miss and refetch), OOM on very large images (sample-size guard), slow network (timeouts + retry policy), and image re-download storms after cache eviction (prefetch).
rubric: Designed a clean, minimal request API
Keyed the cache correctly including size and transformations
Downsampled before decoding and explained the math
Sized the memory cache off memoryClass and counted bytes
Designed disk caching of encoded bytes with eviction
Kept the main thread free of decode
staffAdds: Quantifies: 'a 400 px cell at mdpi is ~ 640 KB decoded; a feed of 40 cells is ~25 MB — that's why the memory cache is sized at 1/8 of a 256 MB heap'
Designs the cache-key collision story and the sampling of cache misses for capacity planning
Plans a plugin point for custom decoders (SVG, animated GIF) without forking the core
Discusses prewarming on cold start and the network budget for the first screen
Defines how to measure: image hit ratio, decode latency p95, OOM-free sessions

items.prompt:
Design a networking library like Retrofit: map a Kotlin interface with annotated methods to typed HTTP calls, add interceptors, adapters, and mocking, and expose it to the app cleanly.

Focus on the client side: interface-to-request mapping, the interceptor chain, how `suspend` functions and reactive types map, and how it's testable. **Set a 45-minute timer and talk out loud.** Tick the requirements as you genuinely cover them.
items.framework: Retrofit is the shape everyone knows, so the interview is about *explaining its moving parts*, not inventing a new one. Expect probing on the interceptor chain and the conversion/adaptation layers.
requirements: Clarify the public API surface (annotated interface)
Explain how a method call becomes an HTTP request
Design the interceptor chain and its order
Design the converter layer (JSON, protobuf) and the adapter layer (suspend, Flow, callback)
Handle auth and token refresh
Design retries with backoff and error mapping
Explain how it integrates with a coroutine scope / lifecycle
Design testability: fake interceptors, mock server, fakes
Handle cancellation of in-flight requests
Cover logging and observability (stetho-style)
Design cache control / conditional requests
Discuss how the client handles timeouts and connectivity
Mention multi-base-URL support
Close with explicit trade-offs
items.referenceAnswer:
#### The core idea
A Kotlin interface like `interface Api { @GET("feed") suspend fun feed(): FeedResponse }`. The library builds a proxy implementation at runtime: each interface method is parsed into a `RequestSpec` (method, path, query, headers, body type, return type), then a `ServiceMethod` knows how to build the request and how to adapt the response.

#### The interceptor chain
An ordered chain, mirroring OkHttp: `Application interceptors → retryAndFollowUp → bridge → network interceptors → callServer`. Two layers of interceptors is the key design decision — application interceptors see the logical request/response (retries, caching, auth), network interceptors see the actual wire bytes (logging, gzip). Order matters: auth must run before retry so a 401-then-refresh-then-retry works.

#### Converter vs adapter
Two separate responsibilities that people conflate:
- **Converter** turns a `ResponseBody` into your type (`MoshiConverterFactory`, `ProtoConverterFactory`). Selected by `contentType` + return type.
- **Adapter** turns a `Call` into the return type of the interface method: `suspend`, `Flow`, `Deferred`, or a callback. `suspend` is implemented by an `enqueue` that resumes the coroutine, and cancels the call on coroutine cancellation.

#### Auth
A dedicated auth interceptor that reads a token provider, attaches the header, and on 401 triggers a single-flight token refresh (ds-0018) before retrying once. Tokens never touch the repository layer.

#### Error handling
Wrap network errors into a typed `ApiException { code, message, body }` mapping: `IOException` → retryable, 5xx → retryable with backoff, 4xx → not retryable except 401/408/429. A `Result<T>` or sealed `ApiResult` return is the idiomatic app-facing shape.

#### Testability
The interceptor chain is the seam: a fake application interceptor can return canned responses without touching the network; `MockWebServer` (bt-0035) exercises the full stack with real HTTP. The interface is mocked with MockK for unit tests. The library itself should never hard-code a scope — the caller owns the `CoroutineScope` so tests can use `runTest`.

#### Observability
A logging interceptor (request line, headers, body, duration) and a metrics hook for latency/error/success counters. Gzip and `Accept-Encoding` handling in the bridge layer.

#### Cancellation
`enqueue`/`await` returns a handle; cancelling the coroutine or job cancels the underlying OkHttp `Call`. Partially received bodies are aborted. This is what prevents slow requests from piling up on fling-cancelled screens.

#### Trade-offs
Interface proxy buys type safety and readability at the cost of reflection/proxies and magic. A hand-rolled `ApiClient` with explicit methods is more debuggable but verbose. You'd choose per team: small APIs → explicit client; large typed APIs → Retrofit-style.
rubric: Designed a two-layer interceptor chain and justified the order
Mapped errors into typed results with a retry policy
staffAdds: Quantifies the concurrency: 'each call pool-bounded; an unbounded OkHttp pool on a feed screen can open 100 sockets — cap and reuse connections'
Plans the migration of a codebase from callbacks to suspend without a big bang
Considers the API-contract story: generated clients vs hand-written, and how the interface doubles as documentation
Defines metrics that gate releases: p95 latency, error rate by endpoint, timeout rate
Designs per-feature base URLs and per-flavor clients (staging vs prod) with no code changes
